instructional_purpose: Teaches that a single negative particle carries two dialect-indexed syntactic profiles: under one it operates on a verbless clause the way the frozen negative copula does, under the other it negates without touching the clause's own case assignment. Supplies the inventory of structural configurations that cancel the operative profile and shows the same clause parsed twice, once under each profile.
concepts_taught: one invariable particle with two register-indexed operativity profiles
operative profile (ما الحجازية): first clause member nominative, second driven to accusative
non-operative profile (ما التميمية): both members keep the default nominative of a verbless clause

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The particle can be assigned a governing profile modelled on the frozen negative copula, keeping the first clause member nominative and marking the second accusative.
Under the rival profile the particle negates with no case consequence and both members stay nominative.
Both profiles are attested and neither is treated as ungrammatical; the ranking between them is a judgement of eloquence grounded in scriptural attestation, not a correctness verdict.
Fronting the predicate before the subject cancels the operative profile absolutely.
An added particle immediately following the negator blocks the operation.
The exceptive particle standing before the predicate forces the nominative.
A fourth cancelling condition involving stacked negation exists, but the lesson states it without content.
The non-operative profile is the ancestor of case-free negation in a modern spoken variety.
Where the predicate carries no visible exponent, the two profiles are indistinguishable in the written record.

instructional_purpose: Makes the operator-and-operand relation explicit as the theory standing behind every case and mood exponent, then sets out two classical accounts of what may count as an operator - one admitting only identifiable surface words, the other admitting abstract meaning - and shows that the accounts agree on the surface exponents while disagreeing about their justification.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Every case or mood exponent is attributed to an operator; this axiom is shared by both accounts and is the foundation of the whole analysis.
Operators must be identifiable surface words, and where none is visible one is posited.
Abstract meaning may itself operate, with the surface particle serving only as its indicator.
In the vocative the calling particle operates on the called nominal, or alternatively the calling sense does.
The operator of the topic in a verbless clause is the abstract state of clause-initiality, or alternatively the comment itself.
The cognate accusative is governed by its verb directly, or alternatively by the meaning of the action with the verb as a mere sign.
The two accounts assign identical surface exponents; the divergence concerns justification, not output.
The emphatic particle operates on the clause subject only, while the predicate holds its nominative from elsewhere.
The two traditions are characterised as favouring attested hearing versus extended analogy respectively.
Neither account is presented as having prevailed over the other.

instructional_purpose: Presents the class of verbs whose paradigm is lexically incomplete - locked to one stem, to one person, or to the imperative alone - and works through the individual members, each showing a differently shaped gap. Motivates the gaps by the specialised, non-eventive meanings the members carry and closes with a matrix keyed by which cells are missing.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A subclass of verbs is lexically restricted to a subset of paradigm cells; the remaining cells are absent from the language, not merely infrequent.
The negative copula exists only on the past stem yet expresses present-time negation, and it still inflects for person, number, and gender.
The verb of expectation has neither imperfect nor imperative and takes a complement built from the subordinator plus an imperfect.
The praise and blame pair take no inflection at all and are followed by a general subject and then a specified nominal in fixed order.
The praise and blame pair are verbs.
The summons word is invariable for every addressee under one dialectal treatment and inflects for gender and number under the other.
The wishing verb has past and imperfect but no imperative, because wishing cannot be commanded.
One blessing verb is restricted to the third person past and reserved for a single referent.
Three exception words function alternately as verbs assigning accusative and as prepositions assigning genitive, with no imperfect or imperative in the exceptive use.
Paradigm gaps arise because the missing cells would be semantically empty.
Because a blocked cell is template-licensed but non-existent, a generator must consult a per-lexeme block list rather than infer the gap from root or template shape.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A circumstantial accusative may restate what its verb already asserts, contributing emphasis rather than information.
The confirming element is derived from the verb's own root, either as a verbal noun or as an active participle.
Removing the element loses emphasis only, and this is the stated membership test.
The same accusative may be filed as a cognate accusative or as a confirming circumstantial, and both classifications are current.
The two classifications are distinguished by which question the element is taken to answer.
When an adjective modifies the element, the circumstantial classification is the more natural one.
An element annexed to a following genitive specifies a kind and therefore leaves the confirming class.
The confirming element carries the accusative under either classification.
Root identity between a verb and a following accusative is not by itself decisive; the informativeness judgement decides.
The scriptural instances cited here are read as confirming under this analysis, while other classifications of the same passages exist.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The particle belongs to the emphatic family: it marks its subject accusative and leaves the predicate nominative.
Its most frequent sense expresses hope for an outcome that is both possible and desired.
The same particle expresses apprehension when the outcome is undesired, the discriminator being desirability read from context.
In classical registers the particle carries a purpose sense equivalent to a final subordinator.
Some scriptural occurrences admit both the hope and the purpose reading, and both are treated as legitimate rather than one being an error.
One tradition tended to foreground the hope reading while some commentators of the other foregrounded the purposive reading in divine contexts.
The purpose sense narrowed over the centuries as dedicated final subordinators took it over.
In modern spoken varieties the particle is largely replaced by possibility words and survives mainly as a frozen first-person form.
The particle is distinguished from the wish particle by the attainability of the outcome.
Sense selection cannot be read off the form, since the particle and its case profile are identical across all three senses.

instructional_purpose: Partitions one high-frequency negative particle into six syntactically distinct functions, each with its own environment, its own effect on the following word, and its own diagnostic cue, then supplies an ordered decision procedure for choosing among them.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The particle has six distinct syntactic functions distinguished by environment rather than by any difference in form.
Before an indicative imperfect with no special context it negates the verb without changing its mood.
Before a bare indefinite noun it negates the whole genus, and that noun is fixed on fatha without nunation.
When the noun after generic negation is modified or is the first term of an annexation it takes the regular accusative instead.
The predicate of a generic negation remains nominative.
Before a second-person imperfect in the jussive it forms a prohibition.
In the correlative frame the second occurrence coordinates, and both coordinated members share the case assigned to the first.
In the fixed complement frame after a preventing verb the particle adds no negation.
The particle preceding a swearing verb in one scriptural opening is redundant rather than negating.
After a verb of fearing, a negated complement is claimed to convey the opposite of its literal negation.
After an oath formula the particle negates the oath's content and the verb keeps the indicative.
The ordered diagnostic resolves the six functions, but two of its steps depend on prior mood knowledge or on recognising a fixed construction, so the ordering is not fully surface-driven.

recognition_criteria: an oath formula immediately preceding, cueing the oath-answer function
a second-person imperfect ending in sukun or with the plural nun dropped, cueing prohibition
an indicative imperfect with its final short vowel or plural nun intact, cueing plain verbal negation
a bare indefinite noun carrying fatha and no nunation, cueing generic negation
a second occurrence of the particle introduced by the coordinator, cueing correlative coordination
the fixed preventing-verb frame with a subordinated complement, cueing the redundant occurrence
procedures: check first for a preceding oath formula
then check whether the following verb is jussive and second person
then check for a coordinated second occurrence of the particle
then check whether a noun rather than a verb follows
then check for the fixed preventing-verb frame
otherwise default to plain verbal negation
for a noun, decide between the fatha-fixed and regular-accusative treatments according to whether the noun is bare, modified, or annexed
